text: An Endonuclease from Escherichia coli That Introduces Single Polynucleotide Chain Scissions in Ultraviolet-irradiated DNA\*
(Received for publication, July 3, 1974, and in revised form, September 18, 1975)
Miroslav Radman‡ From the Biological Laboratories, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138

An endonuclease that makes single polynucleotide chain scissions in ultraviolet-irradiated DNA has been purified from Escherichia coli. The activity has the following properties: (a) unirradiated DNA is aylitt sgotttakwheeiato; no requirement for divalent cations and the activity is not affected by the addition of EDTA; $( d )$ the $\mathbf { p H }$ optimum is approximately 7; (e) the activity is inhibited by $1 \ \mathbf { M } \ \mathbf { N a C l }$ , single strand DNA, transfer RNA and double strand DNA; $( f )$ the sedimentation coefficient, $\pmb { \mathscr { s } } _ { 2 0 , w } ,$ is approximately 2.6; $( g )$ it is a basic protein. The enzyme is tentatively named $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli endonuclease III. The physiological function of the endonuclease has not yet been established.

This study represents an initial attempt to isolate and characterize enzymes involved in correction of mismatched base pairs in DNA. Such local irregularities in the double strand structure of DNA can arise either as a result of the reaction of mutagenic chemicals or radiation with DNA, or as a consequence of the formation of hybrid DNA during genetic recombination (for review, see Ref. 1). Mismatches, i.e. noncomplementary base pairs, will occur during recombination whenever the hybrid region includes portions of the parental molecules containing different genetic markers (2, 3). In such instances, genetic markers which are single base pair substitutions will produce single base pair mismatches, whereas insertion or deletion will produce extensive regions of mispairing, i.e. loops.

There is strong evidence for the existence of cellular errorcorrecting mechanisms for DNA. The most thoroughly studied of these is the correction of pyrimidine dimers (reviews: 4-6), which are chemical modifications induced in DNA by ultraviolet irradiation. In Escherichia coli pyrimidine dimers are excised from the DNA (7, 8) following single strand scission (9) by an endonuclease apparently capable of recognizing pyrimidine dimers. Ultraviolet-sensitive mutants have been found which are deficient in this initial step in excision repair (9, 10) and endonucleases have been isolated, from Micrococcus luteus and $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli, which attack only ultraviolet-irradiated DNA (11-13).
Genetic evidence for the correction of single base pair mismatches in $\pmb { \cal E }$ . coli (14-16) is based on progeny analysis

Using labeled heteroduplex λDNA with three single base pair mismatches as substrate, we have been unable to detect in E. coli extracts any major endonucleolytic activity specific for heteroduplex DNA. In an alternative approach, we have used ultraviolet-irradiated DNA in our assay system in order to purify endonucleases specific for damaged DNA and finally to test their activity on mismatched DNA. In this paper we report purification and some properties of one such endonuclease which is capable of introducing single strand breaks only into ultraviolet-irradiated DNA. The enzyme is tentatively named $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli endonuclease III.

Purification of E. coli Endonuclease I

Endonuclease I (26) was purified in parallel with endonuclease III from E. coli W3110 cells as the major $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent, transfer RNAinhibited endonuclease activity (see "Other Methods"). On both DEAE I and DEAE II chromatography the peak endonuclease activity was eluted in a broad peak around $0 . 3 ~ \mathrm { ~ \bf ~ M ~ } \mathrm { \bf ~ K C l }$ and higher. Only peak fractions were pooled and phosphocellulose chromatography was performed as described above. Peak activity was eluted with $\mathbf { 0 . 3 5 \ M }$ Buffer C (Fig. 2). The peak fraction was concentrated by ultrafiltration and electrofocused as described above: only one band of protein could be seen by staining and this coincided with the endonuclease I activity. Endonuclease I focused very close to cytochrome c $( \mathbf { p I } \ \sim \ \mathbf { 1 0 } )$ . Endonuclease I isolated in this work has been compared with endonuclease I purified and kindly provided by Dr. G. Bernardi and found to exhibit the same properties.

DISCUSSION

This work documents the existence in $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli of an endonuclease that introduces single polynucleotide chain scissions in ultraviolet-irradiated DNA. The enzyme has been purified considerably and some of its properties have been studied. In the absence of relevant knowledge concerning involvement of this nuclease in cellular processes, the enzyme described in this work is tentatively named $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli endonuclease III (Initially, this designation was used by Meselson and Yuan (21) for the restriction endonuclease- $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { K } }$ , but has since been changed (35).

Upon fractionation of $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli cell extracts, several endonucleolytic activities specific for ultraviolet irradiated DNA can be detected (13). ' In addition to endonuclease III, a dialyzable, low molecular weight endonuclease has recently been isolated (13) and still another "ultraviolet endonuclease" activity has been purified partially.
Comparisons between Endonuclease III and Known E. coli Endonucleases

Comparison with Endonuclease I—Endonuclease I has been purified in this work to (or close to) homogeneity as described under "Methods." Purified endonuclease I and endonuclease III have two properties in common: both are inhibited by transfer RNA (26, and Fig. 7) and both are basic proteins of pI around 10 (see "Methods").

Yet, when tested in parallel (this work), they differ in several respects: (a) endonuclease I activity requires $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g } ^ { \mathbf { 2 } + }$ (26), whereas endonuclease III activity does not; (b) under reaction conditions described under "Methods," the purified endonuclease I does not preferentially break the ultraviolet-irradiated DNA when both irradiated and nonirradiated $\phi \mathbf { X 1 7 4 }$ RF-I DNA are used as the substrate; (c) endonuclease I attacks single-stranded $\phi \mathbf { X } 1 7 4$ DNA and native unirradiated DNA, both of which are resistant to attack by endonuclease II; (d) endonuclease I and endonuclease III have been purified in parallel from a wild type $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli extract and a satisfactory separation achieved at the phosphocellulose chromatography stage (Fig. 2); (e) endonuclease I and endonuclease III have been purified in parallel from $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli 1100 endo $I ^ { \star }$ mutant (17), where the level endonuclease III is comparable to that of the wild type $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli, while the level of endonuclease I activity, although detectable, is much lower than in the wild type extracts; $( \pmb { \hat { f } } )$ the activity of the purified endonuclease I survives heat treatment $4 5 ^ { \circ }$ for $3 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ which completely inactivates the activity of endonuclease III. In conclusion, it is unlikely that endonuclease I and endonuclease III are the same enzyme.

Comparison with Endonuclease $\pmb { I I }$ —Endonuclease II from $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ . coli breaks down alkylated DNA by introducing predominantly single strand breaks (36). Endonuclease II and endonuclease III are similar in several respects: $( a )$ both enzymes are apparently specific for an altered DNA; (b) both enzymes are active in the absence of divalent cations; (c) using the Assay II, some preference for ultraviolet-irradiated DNA has been detected\* in a partially purified fraction of endonuclease II. However, this low activity could be due to a contaminating enzyme.

The principal apparent differences between the two enzymes are: $( a )$ no inhibition by transfer RNA of the weak activity on ultraviolet-irradiated DNA of endonuclease II' nor of its activity towards alkylated DNA (36); (b) endonuclease II is stimulated by $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g } ^ { \mathbf { a } + }$ and is inhibited by EDTA (36); (c) endonuclease II when added in excess apparently makes a limited number of breaks in both single-stranded and doublestranded DNA (33); endonuclease III does not (Figs. 4 and 5); $( d )$ isoelectric focusing in liquid column indicates that endonuclease II may be an acidic protein (33), while endonuclease III is a basic protein. Since, (i) the properties of endonuclease II have been determined by using its activity on alkylated DNA as the assay, (ii) endonuclease III has not been tested with alkylated DNA, and (iii) the purity of endonuclease II preparations is uncertain (33), most of the comparisons listed above may be subject to revision.

The estimates of the sedimentation coefficient, $\scriptstyle \pmb { s _ { 2 0 , w } } ,$ of endonuclease I, endonuclease II, and endonuclease III lie between 2.5 and 3.6 (3638), suggesting a similar size of these three endonucleases.

Comparison with Restriction Endonuclease-K-Restriction endonuclease- $\mathbf { K }$ , which can be isolated from $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli strains used in this work, degrades unmodified "foreign" DNA in the presence of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g } ^ { 2 + }$ , S-adenosylmethionine, and ATP, by double strand scissions (21). Endonuclease III shows no activity toward unmodified λDNA (results not shown) and the addition of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g ^ { 2 + } }$ , $\pmb { S } .$ adenosylmethionine, and ATP has no effect upon its activity. Restriction endonuclease- $\mathbf { \nabla } \kappa$ is a very large enzyme with a sedimentation coefficient $\pmb { s } _ { \pmb { \imath 0 } , \pmb { \imath \imath } }$ of approximately 12 (21). In conclusion, restriction endonuçlease-K and endonuclease III appear to be distinct enzymes.

Comparison with Other $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli Endonucleases—E. coli exonuclease $\mathbf { V }$ which is coded by the recB and recC genes has an endonucleolytic activity on single-stranded circular DNA (39). This activity is dependent on the presence of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g } ^ { \mathbf { 2 } + }$ ions and does not degrade ultraviolet-irradiated circular duplex DNA. Another endonucleolytic activity, called endonuclease A3, has been partially purified recently from $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli extracts (40). Endonuclease A3 attacks single-stranded DNA in the absence of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g ^ { 2 + } }$ ions and shows some nicking activity on ultraviolet-irradiated duplex DNA. The absence of endonuclease III activity on the single-stranded $\phi X 1 7 4$ phage DNA (Fig. 5) distinguishes endonuclease III from exonuclease $\mathbf { V }$ and endonuclease A3.

A dialyzable, low molecular weight endonuclease which is specific for the ultraviolet-irradiated DNA recently has been partially purified from $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli extracts (13). The activity of this enzyme, called $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli ultraviolet-endonuclease, was not found in the extracts of the uurA - and uurB- excision repair-deficient mutants, which suggests its implication in the repair of pyrimidine dimers. Braun and Grossman (13) also detected a major nondialyzable ultraviolet endonuclease activity which was found present also in the uurA, uurB, and uurC mutants. Although the $\pmb { \cal E }$ coli ultraviolet endonuclease was not purified and studied extensively, it seems unlikely that endonuclease III and ultraviolet endonuclease are the same enzymes because (a) we have been able to monitor ultraviolet endonuclease activity which was dialyzable under our conditions as well; (b) the two enzyme activities do not co-purify on DEAE-cellulose chromatography; (c) ultraviolet endonuclease is not inhibited by transfer RNA;6 $( d )$ endonuclease II has not the salt requirement characteristic of ultraviolet endonuclease; (e) AB1886 uurA6 mutant shows normal levels of the endonuclease III activity up to the Fraction V (see Table I) of our purification scheme; $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { O } }$ artificially constructed heteroduplexes with λDNA in which only one strand is ultraviolet-irradiated, are nicked by $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli ultraviolet endonuclease only in the irradiated strand,' whereas endonuclease III introduces nicks in both strands of the heteroduplex;' $( { \pmb g } )$ extensive photoreactivation with Micrococcus luteus photoreactivation enzymes decreases, but does not eliminate, the sensitivity of ultraviolet-irradiated DNA to endonuclease III (results not shown).

Possible Roles for Endonuclease III

Introduction of single strand breaks in ultraviolet irradiated DNA (9, 10) is the first step in the process of repair by excision (7, 8) and resynthesis (41) of ultraviolet-induced pyrimidine dimers in vivo: some ultraviolet-sensitive mutants of $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ coli (uur mutants) have been found to be deficient in the initial "incision" step (9) and consequently, pyrimidine dimers are not removed from the DNA (review: Ref. 4). We have not yet tested all these ultraviolet-sensitive mutants for the presence of endonuclease III. This will require a partial purification of the enzyme from each mutant since several specific endonucleolytic activities have been observed using ultravioletirradiated DNA as the substrate (see "Discussion").
In addition to pyrimidine dimers, ultraviolet light induces several classes of lesions (42), which may be recognized by the endonuclease III.

Finally, the possibility exists that endonuclease II may be an enzyme which can recognize mismatched base pairs in general. Initially, endonuclease III was detected and purified to the phosphocellulose step using as substrate.a mixture of homoduplex λDNA and heteroduplex λDNA with three single base pair mismatches' and a weak preferential cutting of the heteroduplex DNA was detected in the alkaline sucrose velocity gradients. Similar low activity was observed when λDNA was ultraviolet-irradiated with a dose yielding only 3 to 6 pyrimidine dimers per molecule (results not shown), probably due to the inhibitory presence of excess of nonsubstrate DNA (Fig. 7). Thus, a new, more sensitive assay must be designed to investigate the possible recognition of single base pair mismatches of endonuclease III. The investigation of the types of distortion in the DNA structure which are recognized by endonuclease III and the screening of mutants deficient in its activity should furnish more information about the biological role of endonuclease III.
